pfmatch

Matching 990-PF grant recipients (Form 990-PF Part XIV Table 3a, “grants paid during the year”) to the IRS Business Master File to recover recipient EINs.

The record-linkage machinery is npmatch: normalization, blocking, comparison, hierarchical scoring, the veto layer, and YES / MAYBE / NO tiering are all used unchanged. This package holds only what is specific to the 990-PF grant context.

Install 

# npmatch first — pfmatch Imports it
install.packages("../npmatch", repos = NULL, type = "source")
install.packages(".",          repos = NULL, type = "source")

# suggested: retrieval and the variable dictionary
remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/panel990")
remotes::install_github("Nonprofit-Open-Data-Collective/concordance990")

The data source

Grants come from the NCCS e-file (ef2) release, retrieved through panel990, which owns release resolution and defaults to the current published version and to parquet:

pf_efilepf_fetch(years = 2015:2025)       # panel990 picks the release
pf_efilepf_build(out = "inputs/grants.csv")   # schema = "v2", dedup = TRUE
pf_source_provenance()
#> $efile_version  "v3_1"
#> $efile_root     "https://nccs-efile.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/public/efilepf_v3_1/"
#> $efile_format   "parquet"
#> $concordance_version "2.0.3"

Column names are the concordance990 v2 research variables (PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_NAME_ORG_L1, ORG_EIN, …), documented in the 990-PF data dictionary. pf_concordance_vars() reads them from the installed concordance rather than hardcoding them, and warns if pfmatch expects a name the concordance has renamed — so a dictionary change surfaces as a warning instead of a column that silently reads as all-missing.

A note on the earlier source

This package was prototyped against GT’s Data Mart extract, whose columns carry the concordance990 v1 names (SIGOCPYRPNAM, SIGOCPYRBNBN1, FILEREIN, …). Those are superseded. The GT extract is also truncated at the recent end — 2024 is under-represented roughly tenfold and 2025 is absent — so it is kept only in inputs/archive-gt/ for reproducing pre-migration artifacts, never for measurement. pf_read_grants() refuses to concatenate the two vintages.

Readers accept either naming through an internal resolver, so files built before the migration still work; new code should use the v2 names.

Duplicate and superseded filings

pf_efilepf_build() deduplicates by default. The unit is (EIN2, TAX_YEAR, group flag, partial flag) — a filing can only supersede another covering the same reporting context — and within a context identical filings collapse, an amended filing supersedes the original, and filings that disagree with no amendment to settle them are all kept and flagged.

On the 17,560,767-row corpus that removes 307,568 rows (1.75%) across 9,882 of 977,677 filings, leaving 5 contexts flagged for review. Two properties are deliberate and tested:

  • a short-period return is never dropped for sharing a tax year with a full-year one — they cover different periods, and in 97 of 310 such pairs the partial return reports more grants
  • the dedup unit is not keyed on the tax period, because in 18 units an amendment corrected the period dates; keying on it would stop the amendment superseding its original

990-PF filers do not file group returns (RETURN_GROUP_X is FALSE on every row), but the flag stays in the key so the behaviour holds if that changes.

Rows are addressed by OBJECTID | TABLE_ID, the published ef2 row key — OBJECTID identifies the filing, TABLE_ID counts rows within it. Verified unique across all 17.5M rows.

Use

Four stages, or one call:

library(pfmatch)

res <- pf_run(grants = "inputs", bmf = ".../bmf_2026_01_processed.csv")

# or stage by stage, when you want to cache between them
prep <- pf_prepare(grants, dedup = "fuzzy")        # read -> repair -> scope -> dedup
ref  <- pf_reference(bmf)                          # build or load the cached bundle
lnk  <- pf_link(prep, ref, batch_size = 25000)     # cascade -> self-guard -> propagate
adj  <- pf_adjudicate(lnk, bmf)                    # the review sheet
stage does key functions
pf_prepare() read grants, repair name-in-street, standardize the recipient-status field, decide scope, collapse to distinct recipient identities pf_read_grants(), pf_prepare_grants(), pf_standardize_status(), pf_dedup(), pf_recipients()
pf_reference() read + normalize the BMF, name frequency, token IDF, blocking index, acronym/prefix keys — cached, and excluded from match timings pf_build_reference()
pf_link() the staged blocking cascade in checkpointed batches, self-match guard, then propagate each identity’s result to every grant row pf_staged_passes(), pf_recovery_passes(), pf_run_batches(), pf_propagate_matches()
pf_adjudicate() candidate sheet with BMF and foundation context, optional purpose tiebreak pf_candidate_frame(), pf_build_org_text(), pf_purpose_tiebreak()

Results are summarized by pf_report(), pf_status(), and pf_crosstab().

Repository layout 

R/               the package
data/            nteev2.rda — the only bundled data (built by data-raw/)
data-raw/        make-nteev2.R
inputs/          grant CSVs, 990 Part III extracts, NTEE source files  (not shipped)
data-dev/        derived artifacts, caches, checkpoints                (not shipped)
dev/             benchmarks, probes, findings                          (not shipped)

inputs/ was called data/ until the package skeleton was added; it holds 600 MB+ of source files and had to give up the name to R’s reserved data/.

What is specific to this problem

1. R/recipient-type.R — standardizing PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_STAT

Column (c) of the grants table asks the filer for the “foundation status of recipient” and the IRS supplies no controlled vocabulary. Across 155,000 sample grants the field carries ~1,400 distinct spellings of about eight concepts.

pf_standardize_status() is a rule cascade, not a lookup table, so unseen spellings land in the right bucket. Two normalizations do most of the work:

  • section collapsing — 501(c)(3), 501C 3, 501 C 3, 501c3 all become the single token 501C3; likewise 509A1, 170B1A, 4942J3.
  • de-spacing — every pattern is also matched against a space-free copy of the string, so PUB CHAR, PUBLIC CH, and OTHERPUBLICCHARITY are all caught by one pattern.

Order matters: operating foundations are tested before the generic 501(c)(3) rules (an operating foundation is a c3 but is emphatically not a public charity), and government before the bare-PUBLIC fallback (so “PUBLIC UNIVERSITY” does not become a public charity).

level share of 155k
public_charity 70.5%
other_unknown 20.6%
nonprofit_other 4.3%
individual 3.6%
foundation_pf 1.1%

Coverage is 98.6%; the 1.4% residual is text that answers a different question (“PAID”, “CASH”, “VARIOUS”, “ACTIVE”, “SEE GENERAL EXPLANATION”). Use pf_status_audit(x, detail = "unrecognized") to see what a new extract still misses before trusting the split.

A finer recipient_type_detail is carried alongside, because other_unknown mixes cases that behave very differently — government and foreign can never be in the BMF, while blank and unrecognized are usually organizations the filer simply did not code. Only the detail level drives scope (pf_oos_details()).

Two judgment calls worth knowing about:

  • NC is the standard shorthand for a non-charity recipient — the filers who spell it out write “NC: NON-EXEMPT”. It says what the recipient is not, so it is not promoted to “nonprofit (other)”, but it stays in scope: a 501(c)(4) or a taxable entity may still hold a BMF row.
  • Equivalency determinations are how a US foundation grants to a foreign org with no IRS ruling, so they are classified foreign and held out of the match.

2. R/prepare.R — recipient name and address

The data dictionary settles the name-field question. There are three columns:

  • PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_NAME_PERS — “Recipient Person Name”
  • PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_NAME_ORG_L1 — “…business name line 1”
  • PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_NAME_ORG_L2 — “…business name line 2”

So The two _ORG_L1/_ORG_L2 columns are a two-line wrap of one name, not a main name and a DBA — confirming the working assumption. _NAME_PERS and _ORG_L1 never co-occur (0 of 155,000 rows carry both), so the recipient name is a straight coalesce.

_NAME_PERS is not a usable individual flag: filers routinely put organizations in it (“World Central Kitchen”, “Surfrider Foundation”), which is why scope is decided from PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_STAT instead.

Line 2, when present, is one of four things and each is handled separately:

line 2 is n (5k sample) handling
a genuine continuation 2,047 joined onto line 1 as an alternate name
a duplicate of line 1 983 dropped
a care-of / attention line 735 dropped (address data in a name field)
an FBO beneficiary 27 dropped, trailing FBO stripped from line 1

The joined continuation is carried in npmatch’s dba slot. That is a deliberate reuse rather than a claim that it is a DBA: np_compare() scores the full name/DBA cross-product and keeps the best, so a record can match on either the truncated line-1 form or the complete one — whichever the BMF happens to hold. It earns its keep: the exact-name-dba pass resolves 86 YES on the 5k sample.

Other handling: 4-digit ZIPs are repaired (a dropped New-England leading zero), spelled-out state names are folded to postal codes, and a state value that is not a US postal jurisdiction marks the record foreign. PF_15_G_PAID_RECIP_ADDR_CNTR (country) is in the schema but empty throughout the sample, so foreign detection has to come from the state field.

looks_personal is a diagnostic only and never drives scope: a 2-3 token name with no institutional token and a positive person signal (a single-letter initial, or a common given name). It fires on 0.7% of YES matches and 18% of out-of-sample rows, which is the right direction.

3. R/match.R — the cascade

Full walkthrough in dev/CASCADE.md: what is compared, the scoring formula, all eleven passes, the vetoes, and how a grant lands in YES / MAYBE / NO. The short version:

Both sides carry two name slots, so name similarity is the best of a cross-product — max(name×name, name×dba, dba×name, dba×dba). The query dba is recip_name_alt, the untruncated line1+line2 form. Address is not one comparison either: seven location signals are emitted and the geo score takes the strongest, never a sum.

score = 0.60 · name  +  0.40 · geo

geo   = max( 1.00·zip9,  0.95·street,  0.90·zip5,  0.90·pobox,
             0.55·zip3,  0.50·city,    0.20·state )

Taking the max means correlated address fields cannot double-count and a wrong city cannot pull down a ZIP-confirmed match. Fuzzy similarities are floored to 0 below jw_threshold (0.85) — reclin2’s threshold= is the Winkler prefix boost, not a cutoff, so unrelated strings otherwise leak ~0.5 into every score.

Eleven passes run cheapest-first and a query resolved to YES leaves the pending set, so expensive passes only see the residue. Stage A (exact, state-blocked) resolves the bulk on a few thousand candidates; stages B–D spend two orders of magnitude more candidates on the tail.

Tiering is score ≥ 0.78 → YES, ≥ 0.65 → MAYBE, else NO, with two demotions from YES to MAYBE: a margin under 0.05 to the runner-up (an ambiguity brake — something else is nearly as good), and a soft veto. The soft vetoes that matter here are affiliate_suffix (candidate ends FOUNDATION / ENDOWMENT / AUXILIARY / BOOSTERS and the query does not) and government_entity.

These thresholds are npmatch defaults, fitted on SAM/USASpending — not on 990-PF data. What is worth re-tuning, what the current label set can support, and why tier boundaries cannot be tuned on MAYBE-only labels: dev/OPTIMIZATION-PLAN.md.

3a. Two pass configurations

pf_staged_passes() is the production cascade (state-blocked bulk plus a cheap cross-state exact sweep) and pf_default_passes() is the state-free measurement baseline. On 5,000 grants the staged lean configuration is 1.48x faster, uses 2.0x fewer candidate pairs, and returns 13 more YES matches. See dev/SCALE-PLAN.md for the full comparison.

The single most efficient pass is A1, which blocks on name + ZIP5 with no state key: 1,834 matches from 8,285 candidates. It is also what makes state blocking safe, because it catches the “filer typed the wrong state” cases (right city, right ZIP, wrong two-letter code) without any cross-state sweep.

The unblocked token sweep is off by default (sweep = "lean"). Measured, it generated 59% of all candidate pairs and produced zero additional YES matches — its only product is extra MAYBE candidates. Turn it on with sweep = "full" when filling the adjudication queue matters more than runtime.

3b. The state-free baseline and why it exists

npmatch’s default cascade blocks every pass on state and only opens up to a cross-state token pass at the end. That is right when query and reference are the same establishment; it is wrong here, because a New York foundation routinely funds a California charity and the address the filer types is whatever was on the check. Every pass in pf_default_passes() is state-free:

pass criterion
exact-name name == name, any state
exact-name-dba name == dba, any state
exact-dba-name dba == name, any state
exact-dba-dba dba == dba, any state
token-any shared distinctive token (IDF-pruned), any state

“No blocking” cannot mean a full cross product — 5,000 grants against 1.9M BMF rows is 9.6 billion pairs. What is dropped is geographic blocking. Candidates are still generated by exact name keys and by a shared distinctive name token, which is a recall device rather than a geographic constraint. State is used only downstream, as scoring evidence.

pf_build_reference() does the one-time BMF work (read, normalize, name frequency, token IDF, blocking index) and caches it, so it is excluded from the match timings. pf_match_grants() times only the cascade.

4. R/report.R — the four-way outcome

  • YES — one candidate cleared the auto-accept threshold with a clear lead
  • MAYBE — candidates surfaced but need adjudication (below threshold, a near-tie with the runner-up, or a soft veto)
  • NO — no candidate surfaced, or the best one scored below the review floor
  • OOS — out of sample: a natural person, a government unit, or a foreign organization. Nothing to find, so not counted as a miss.

pf_report() prints the outcome split, the outcome x recipient-type crosstab, geographic-agreement diagnostics, the per-pass cascade table, and the runtime; pf_status(), pf_crosstab(), and pf_geo_agreement() return the frames.

5. R/dyads.R — EIN dyads

A grant reported to EAGLE RANCH may have been paid to EAGLE RANCH FOUNDATION. When both are candidates, the margin brake in §3 fires on a runner-up that is the same body under a second EIN — median margin on affected grants is exactly 0.000, a grant held back for tying with itself.

pf_build_dyads() reads Schedule A Part I line 12g and Schedule R Part II disclosures (2009–2024) and classifies each disclosed pair as substitutable or merely related. pf_link(dyads = ) then collapses substitutable candidates within one grant’s candidate list before selection and re-runs the tiering: 704 MAYBE grants become YES on the 50k run, with nothing moving into NO.

Two rules are not negotiable, both learned the hard way:

  • Direct edges only, never a transitive closure. Connected components over the disclosure graph produce a single component of 66,973 EINs across 56 states.
  • Substitution requires exclusivity. A bare Schedule A edge gave the YMCA Retirement Fund 905 “substitutable” partners — it supports 907 local YMCAs.

dev/DYAD-FINDINGS.md for the evidence, dev/CLUSTER-FINDINGS.md for the negative result that shaped the design.

Benchmarks and development 

PF_SET=1k Rscript dev/run-test-match.R      # the five 1,000-row files
PF_SET=50k Rscript dev/run-test-match.R
PF_SET=100k Rscript dev/run-test-match.R
Rscript dev/run-full-file.R                 # checkpointed production run

The first run builds data-dev/BMF-REFERENCE-BUNDLE.rds (~5 min, 1.3 GB) and reuses it thereafter. Set NPMATCH_DIR / PFMATCH_DIR to relocate.

dev/ scripts use devtools::load_all() rather than library(pfmatch), so they can reach internal and unexported functions. They are not part of the package.

Planning documents: dev/PACKAGE-PLAN.md (what packaging still owes), dev/NPMATCH-PROMOTION-PLAN.md (three modules to move upstream, and one npmatch defect this project found).

Results

The current frozen measurement is dev/BASELINE-2026-10B/, taken on the deduplicated v2 population (inputs/efv2_1k_grants_0*.csv, 4,903 grants):

reference identities YES MAYBE NO clear rate
active, 1,924,822 rows 4,687 2,665 987 1,035 56.86%
augmented, 3,880,431 rows 4,748 2,982 1,041 725 62.81%

Read dev/BASELINE-2026-10B/MANIFEST.md before quoting either: it records what the figures do and do not establish, and the baseline is gated on np_normalize_signature(), so it goes stale when npmatch’s normalizer changes.

This is a clear rate, not an accuracy. Precision on the YES mass has never been measured, because every ground-truth label this project holds came from a cell the pipeline itself produced. To score a configuration rather than argue about its clear rate, use pf_evaluate() and pf_consistency().

Two older read-outs are kept as history and should not be quoted as current: dev/BASELINE-2026-10/ (the same measurement on the undeduplicated v1 population, 63.01% augmented) and dev/BENCHMARK-NOTES.md (54.9%, from before state blocking, the apostrophe fix, the augmented reference and the e-file rebuild — it remains useful for its cost and recipient-type breakdowns).

Audits

dev/AUDIT-FINDINGS.md reports three 100-case manual audits of the NO, OOS, and MAYBE tiers, with per-case verdicts in dev/maybe-verdicts.csv. Short version: the NO tier is mostly real nonprofits we failed to reach (13 of 15 web-confirmed EINs are in the BMF), the OOS flag is wrong 24% of the time because column (c) describes the beneficiary rather than the payee, and 63% of MAYBE cases contain the correct EIN in the top five candidates.
